author: honorius

lemma.la: duodecim horas super terram, et duodecim sub terra
lemma.en: twelve hours above the earth and twelve below

original.text: Et vidit Deus lucem, quod esset bona. Hoc est, rationali creaturae intelligere dedit: quam bona sint cuncta, quae per lucem cernit. Et divisit lucem ac tenebras: scilicet ut lux duodecim horas super terram, et duodecim sub terra splendesceret: tenebrae quoque a luce fugatae duodecim horas sub terra totidemque super terram delitescerent.

english.text: And God saw the light, that it was good. That is, he gave the rational creature to understand how good are all the things it discerns by the light. And he divided the light and the darkness: namely, so that the light should shine twelve hours above the earth and twelve below the earth; and the darkness, put to flight by the light, should lie hidden twelve hours below the earth and as many above it.

notes: The literal answer taken as far as it will go: the division is a timetable. The light of the first day travels on a twelve-hour circuit above the earth and twelve below, and the darkness does the reverse, hiding below while the light is above. Bede's difference of place has become a mechanism with hours in it, and there is no privation anywhere in the sentence — the darkness is put to flight by the light and lies hidden, which are things only a body does. On the *ki tov* half Honorius takes the seeing out of God altogether: 'he gave the rational creature to understand how good are all the things it discerns by the light', so the goodness is what we see by the light, not what God saw in it. Nobody else on either bench makes the approval a gift to the beholder.
